questions.stem: A 47-year-old man presented with a fever and constipation for 5 days. He had been nonspecifically unwell for 3 weeks. Two weeks before presentation, he had returned from a 6-month trip to India. On examination he was systemically unwell with rigors and fever >38°C. He had palpable hepatosplenomegaly and generalized abdominal tenderness. Investigations: Total white cell count 3.0 ×109/L Hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL Platelet count 150,000/μL Blood cultures negative at 24 hours He was commenced on intravenous ceftriaxone therapy.
questions.lead_in: What further investigation would have the highest diagnostic yield?

options.text: Computed tomography scan of the abdomen

questions.explanation: Bone marrow culture This patient has a suspected diagnosis of Salmonella Typhi, acquired in India, and has constipation, rather than diarrhea, seen in about 30% of patients. He has developed hepatosplenomegaly and may have bacteremia. Blood and stool cultures should be requested; blood cultures are positive in 40%–80%, stool culture positivity is 30%–40% and although not often performed, bone marrow may have additional yield >90% in more complicated cases or if unresponsive to treatment and can remain positive for >5 days after antibiotic initiation.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q18

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man presented with 3 weeks of fever, headache, malaise, abdominal pain, and constipation. He had returned from a 6-month trip to India 2 weeks before his symptoms began. On examination, he was confused on admission but with no focal neurology or meningism. His temperature was 39.2°C, heart rate 75 beats per minute, blood pressure 110/56 mmHg. A CT scan of the head and lumbar puncture were performed, with normal CSF findings. The CT was unremarkable. He was started empirically on intravenous ceftriaxone, fluid resuscitated, and admitted to the high dependency unit. Three malaria smears at 12-hour intervals were negative. Twenty-four hours after admission he developed worsening abdominal pain, and he had peritonitis on examination. He was taken for an exploratory laparotomy (see image). Blood cultures on admission grew gram-negative rods at 48 hours.
questions.lead_in: What part of the bowel is most likely to be involved?
questions.explanation: Terminal ileum Gastrointestinal perforation, usually at the terminal ileum, is the most serious complication of typhoid infection. It manifests as an acute abdomen or as worsening of abdominal pain accompanied by shock. Perforation is associated with a high mortality risk and needs urgent surgical intervention. (Image from Assessments. In Cohen J, Powderly W , Opal S, eds. Infectious Diseases. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2017.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q38

questions.question: 24. 4 Scenarios, all have same disease and no allergies. What is the one antimicrobial that is recommended in each situation? Scenario 1: 13 year old return from Pakistan, fever, abdo pain and GNB in blood after 18 hours, admitted to PICU. Scenario 2: 21 year old female returned from Thailand unwell but hemodynamically stable. Scenario 3: 41 year old humanitarian worker returned from Haiti with abdo pain and can tolerate oral therapy. Scenario 4: 17 year old return from Pakistan with mild abdo pain and fever and stable, can tolerate PO and be sent home.

parts.text: What is the one antimicrobial recommended in each of the 4 scenarios above?
Name 2 organism genus and species (taxonomically written) that can cause this disease.

questions.model_answer: a) Antimicrobial per scenario: (1) 13yo from Pakistan, severe/PICU: meropenem (carbapenem) IV - Pakistan is the epicenter of extensively drug-resistant (XDR) Salmonella Typhi, resistant to fluoroquinolones, ceftriaxone, and other 3rd-gen cephalosporins, leaving carbapenems as treatment of choice for severe disease from this region. (2) 21yo from Thailand, unwell but stable: IV ceftriaxone (fluoroquinolone resistance also common in Southeast Asia; ceftriaxone remains reliable). (3) 41yo from Haiti, tolerating oral therapy: oral azithromycin (Haiti/Caribbean strains generally fluoroquinolone-susceptible, but azithromycin preferred oral option/or oral fluoroquinolone if susceptible). (4) 17yo from Pakistan, mild, tolerating PO, discharged home: oral azithromycin (avoid oral fluoroquinolone/cephalosporin given XDR strain prevalence from Pakistan). b) Two organisms causing enteric fever (taxonomically written): Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi and Salmonella enterica serovar Paratyphi A.

questions.question: 4 different scenarios of a patient returning from travel (Pakistan, Haiti) with fever and abdominal pain (told it's the same organism).

parts.text: What are 4 empiric antimicrobial agents against this likely organism based on travel and severity (one patient in ICU, one stable but unwell and still vomiting, two patients tolerating PO and can be discharged)
What are two relatively common complications of this infection?
What are the names of two organisms that can cause this syndrome based on currently accepted taxonomy?

questions.model_answer: a) Four empiric agents by scenario/severity: ICU/severe illness - meropenem (or IV ceftriaxone if region without XDR concern); unwell/vomiting requiring admission - IV ceftriaxone or IV azithromycin; two stable patients tolerating PO, discharge candidates - oral azithromycin (or oral fluoroquinolone if strain likely susceptible, e.g. non-South Asian travel history). b) Two common complications: intestinal hemorrhage and intestinal perforation (both from Peyer patch ulceration in the terminal ileum). c) Two organisms by current taxonomy: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi and Salmonella enterica serovar Paratyphi A.

questions.question: An infection occurs in the following individuals. What antimicrobial would you use to treat this infection?

parts.text: 11 year old girl returning from pakistan who is critically ill, febrile in the ICU. She is growing GNB in 4/4 blood cultures.
Another individual returning from Thailand who is unwell enough from fever and vomiting that she needs to be admitted but just needs fluid resuscitation.
20M who was also in Pakistan but he’s well enough that he doesn’t need to be admitted and can tolerate oral antibiotics.
40F who was in Haiti who is well enough that she doesn’t need to be admitted.
What are two organisms that can cause the above conditions with current taxonomy?
What are 2 immune mediated consequences of this infection?

questions.model_answer: a) 11yo critically ill from Pakistan, GNB 4/4 blood cultures: meropenem IV (Pakistan-associated XDR Typhi resistant to fluoroquinolones and ceftriaxone). b) Patient from Thailand, unwell, needing admission for fluids: IV ceftriaxone. c) 20M from Pakistan, stable, tolerating oral: oral azithromycin (avoid oral fluoroquinolone/cephalosporin given regional XDR risk). d) 40F from Haiti, well, not requiring admission: oral azithromycin (or oral fluoroquinolone if strain expected susceptible). e) Two causative organisms (current taxonomy): Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi and Salmonella enterica serovar Paratyphi A. f) Two immune-mediated complications: reactive arthritis and Guillain-Barre syndrome (also glomerulonephritis/hemolytic anemia accepted).

questions.question: You are seeing an 11-year-old girl who has just returned from Pakistan with a febrile illness. Blood cultures return with gram-negative bacilli at 15 hours.

parts.text: What is the genus and species of this organism?
What TWO therapy options would be appropriate and why?
What are two classic, but serious complications of this infection?

questions.model_answer: a) Genus and species: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi. b) Two appropriate therapy options and why: (1) Meropenem IV - given travel to Pakistan, a region with high prevalence of extensively drug-resistant (XDR) S. Typhi resistant to fluoroquinolones and third-generation cephalosporins including ceftriaxone; carbapenem is the reliable empiric choice pending susceptibilities. (2) Azithromycin IV/PO - retains activity against most XDR strains and is a reasonable alternative/step-down option once clinically improving. c) Two classic serious complications: intestinal perforation and gastrointestinal hemorrhage (from ileal Peyer patch ulceration).

questions.question: The following case scenarios relate to typhoid fever. How you would treat a patient from: Pakistan who is sick; Pakistan who is not sick; Other country sick; Other country not sick.

parts.text: Treatment for Pakistan sick
Treatment for Pakistan not sick
Treatment for other country sick
Treatment for other country not sick
Name the bacteria in full nomenclature.
What are 2 complications aside from septic shock.

cohort_answer.text: Pakistan sick: Meropenem. Pakistan not sick: Azithromycin. Non-Pakistan sick: Ceftriaxone. Non-Pakistan not sick: FQ (e.g. cipro) for Sub-Saharan Africa or Azithromycin for South Asia (due to increasing resistance in Asia). Bacteria: Salmonella enterica subspecies enterica serovar Typhi. Complications: Aortitis, osteomyelitis, meningitis, bacteremia, gastroenteritis, bowel perforation, septic joint. (XDR typhoid reported in Iraq, Bangladesh, India, Pakistan - majority from Pakistan; azithromycin typically still susceptible for XDR strains.)
